stimulus.text:
President Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918 (verbatim excerpts):

"I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view."

"II. Absolute freedom of navigation upon the seas, outside territorial waters, alike in peace and in war, except as the seas may be closed in whole or in part by international action for the enforcement of international covenants."

"III. The removal, so far as possible, of all economic barriers and the establishment of an equality of trade conditions among all the nations consenting to the peace and associating themselves for its maintenance."

"IV. Adequate guarantees given and taken that national armaments will be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety."

"XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike."

options.misconception: Nothing in the quoted points punishes Germany. Wilson calls for open diplomacy, free trade, lower arms, and a league of nations.

a military alliance of the victors against future German aggression
options.misconception: Wilson proposes a general association of nations for mutual guarantees, not a victors' alliance aimed at Germany. The points look forward to cooperation, not to a new alliance against one state.

options.text: the restoration of secret treaties between the Allied powers
options.misconception: Point I calls for open covenants and an end to private international understandings. Secret treaties are what Wilson wants to end.

rationales.A: Nothing in the quoted points punishes Germany. Wilson calls for open diplomacy, free trade, lower arms, and a league of nations.
rationales.B: Point I demands open diplomacy, Point III demands free trade, and Point XIV demands a general association of nations. Together they describe a peace built on openness and cooperation.
rationales.C: Wilson proposes a general association of nations for mutual guarantees, not a victors' alliance aimed at Germany. The points look forward to cooperation, not to a new alliance against one state.
rationales.D: Point I calls for open covenants and an end to private international understandings. Secret treaties are what Wilson wants to end.
rationales.general:
1. List what the points ask for. Open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, lower arms, and a general association of nations.
2. Ask what those items share. Each one replaces secrecy, barriers, and arms races with openness and cooperation.
3. Check the punishments. No quoted point takes German territory or demands reparations.
Remember: to name a plan's aim, add up what its parts ask for and leave out what none of them asks for.
